title: Implementing gameplay with GameFramework
subtitle: A component walkthrough for the game team

slides.title:
Implementing gameplay
with GameFramework
slides.lead: Find an actor. Attach behavior. Let the World run it.
slides.caption: Working example: the rotating orientation gizmo
slides.notes: Allow 30 seconds. This is a developer integration walkthrough for teammates who can already import and run a scene. The goal is to show where code belongs and how components become active. The actual Unreal custom export and game factory are deferred until the school environment is available; we will flag that boundary clearly.

slides.title: The rotator example
slides.lead: The scene supplies the actor and mesh. Our component supplies rotation.
slides.caption: Live demo: show the gizmo, then press F4 to reload
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. Show the running Blockout scene and the orientation gizmo first. Locate it before the session, rather than searching during the presentation. The programmer confirmed rotation on the gizmo and previously confirmed that Cube2 rotation and F4 reload did not crash. The manual demo is implemented; no Unreal custom component is responsible for this attachment yet. If the app is unavailable, use a runtime capture made at school, not an invented screenshot.

slides.title: Where your code belongs
rows: Your behavior
Source/Application/Game — custom components and feature systems
Scene setup
Game::ConfigureWorld — attach and configure per-scene behavior
Engine components
GameFramework/Components — reuse meshes, animation, cameras, lights
Runtime
GameApplication — scene loading and the frame loop
slides.caption: New source files must also be included in the generated Game project
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. Open the source tree. SpinComponent is beside Game.cpp today; feature subfolders are an optional organization choice, not an existing mandatory convention. Independent algorithms can also live in game feature folders without inheriting Component. Premake includes game headers and C++ files recursively, but an already generated Visual Studio project must be regenerated or explicitly updated. Leave engine lifecycle and window/render-loop control in GameApplication.

slides.title: Find an actor or create one
points: A new actor needs a visual component to be visible
slides.notes: Allow 60 seconds. The second snippet is illustrative and is not part of the implemented rotator demo. An actor has a transform; adding a mesh or other visual is a separate step. World owns actors, which own components. Returned pointers are borrowed. World currently suffixes repeated actor names rather than rejecting them, so inspect the returned actor's actual name if later lookup matters. Actor is final; extend behavior through components.

slides.title: Attach and configure behavior
slides.caption: C++ type selects the class; the string names this instance
slides.notes: Allow 2 minutes. This is the actual attachment logic, shortened with auto for slide readability. Open Game.cpp and point to ConfigureWorld. AddComponent constructs and attaches the component, then setters configure it. Owner is available after attachment, not in the constructor. Instance names are nonempty and unique within an actor. ConfigureWorld runs on a candidate World before BeginPlay, so dependencies and settings are ready for initialization. Reload creates a fresh World and repeats the attachment. Do not retain the returned pointer across reload.

slides.title: Retrieve existing components
points: Include the engine or game component header
Check for null before using either result
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. The lookup snippet illustrates existing APIs; it is not an extra implemented code block. Include GameFramework/Components/StaticMeshComponent.h and SpinComponent.h. GetComponent returns the first matching C++ type. When several components have the same type, use FindComponent with a name and check the cast. Inside your own component, use GetOwner and GetWorld. Resolve dependencies in BeginPlay after construction when possible. The companion walkthrough includes null-checked usage.

slides.title: The custom component class
slides.caption: Component adds behavior; SceneComponent also adds a spatial offset
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. This is a shortened class outline; show SpinComponent.h for the full class. The parameter is renamed to speed only for brevity, not as a new API. SpinComponent inherits Component because it modifies its owner or a target component rather than needing its own transform. Use SceneComponent when the feature has an actor-relative position or orientation of its own. Our rotator already has setters, a default speed, a target lookup helper, and yaw state. It has no input listener or owned resource that needs an EndPlay override.

slides.title: Component lifecycle
rows: Configure
Defaults and setters establish values before play
BeginPlay
Resolve dependencies and initialize runtime state
Update
Advance enabled behavior on an active actor
EndPlay
Remove subscriptions and release runtime connections
slides.caption: The application and World drive lifecycle calls for you
slides.notes: Allow 2 minutes. Open SpinComponent::BeginPlay: it reads the authored yaw so spinning starts from the existing orientation. Explain that disabled components can still begin play, but enabled/active checks control normal updates. Components that subscribe to input should retain their listener IDs and remove them in EndPlay; this rotator has no subscription. Additions from component callbacks wait for a later collected World frame. Gameplay should not manually call World.BeginPlay or World.Update.

slides.title: Rotation during Update
slides.caption: 45 degrees/second × 0.1 seconds = 4.5 degrees
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. This is the actual Update body, reflowed to fit. State advances with elapsed time, not once by a fixed angle per frame. FullRotationDegrees is 360. Negative speed reverses direction; zero stops it. The setter rejects non-finite speed. The modulo bounds yaw, and negative remainders still represent valid angles. Reading the existing rotation retains pitch and roll. This component writes yaw, so coordinate with any other component that also writes the same target transform.

slides.title: Actor and component transforms
slides.lead: This engine stores rotation as yaw, pitch, roll.
points: Vector x: yaw about Y · y: pitch about X · z: roll about Z
No target name: rotate the actor
Named SceneComponent: rotate its actor-relative offset
slides.caption: A missing or wrong-type named target receives no transform update
slides.notes: Allow 60 seconds. This convention is easy to misread: GetLocalRotationDegrees().x is yaw, not rotation about X. Open Transform.h if needed. The three-argument setter takes yaw, pitch, roll. The actor is the root transform; SceneComponent composes an actor-relative transform. The current demo uses the actor target, which keeps the example simple. Target-name lookup is optional existing behavior. Position and scale are not changed by the rotator.

slides.title: Scene construction and activation
steps: World builder creates the candidate World
slides.caption: Configure settings before activation; reacquire pointers after reload
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. Follow ProcessPendingSceneLoad in GameApplication.cpp. Source conversion returns plain SceneData. BuildWorldFromSceneData creates engine actors and components. ConfigureWorld is the current extension for game behavior. After successful pre-commit construction the runtime clears the old World, commits the candidate, handles camera fallback, and calls BeginPlay. A later load that fails before replacement leaves the old World running; initial loading must succeed. Current scene requests use filesystem paths, not the SceneId mentioned in older guides.

slides.title: One frame in the current runtime
steps: Messages, scene requests, resize and delta time
slides.caption: Your component Update runs inside World::Update
slides.notes: Allow 60 seconds. Keep this high level. The current loop runs Game.Update before World.Update, then audio and coroutine scheduler work, followed by rendering. Delta time is capped at 0.25 seconds. World collects a frame list in actor/component order. Components added from callbacks wait for a later update; components added by Game.Update before World.Update can be collected that frame. Do not depend on incidental update order for a feature that should exchange intent explicitly.

slides.title: Integrating team features
rows: Player
Controller records intent; movement changes the actor
Enemy
A component connects decisions to movement and animation
Navmesh
Pathfinding stays separate; a component requests and follows paths
VFX
A component connects the effect to actor transforms and lifecycle
slides.caption: Design examples — these gameplay features are not implemented by this demo
slides.notes: Allow 90 seconds. Explain the division between an independent algorithm and the component integrating it. Pathfinding can operate on navigation data without inheriting Component; an actor component connects its output to movement. Existing skeletal mesh and AnimatorComponent types can be reused. This engine does not acquire a complete player, navmesh, physics, or VFX system just by adding a component. Renderer or service integration may still be required by the feature itself.
